clue.text: Sure indications, two of which are apparent in this puzzle

definitions.text: Sure indications, two of which are apparent in this puzzle

parts.note: read straight, this is the doctor's or the forecaster's phrase for evidence that things are going the right way

parts.words: two of which are apparent in this puzzle
parts.note: the setter means it literally: the black squares draw two plus shapes, and the word PLUS is written inside two of the answers as well

explanation.surface: Someone pointing out that the encouraging omens are there for anyone who looks.
explanation.walkthrough: The black squares of this grid make two plus shapes, and PLUS is spelled out inside two answers, so the clue is counting the setter's own handiwork.
explanation.definitionFit: A plus sign is a positive sign, and 'sure indications' is the everyday phrase for omens you can rely on — both senses live in the same two words.

clue.text: Work on academic cancelling of tyrant

indicators.note: To cancel is to strike out, so whatever is named next gets struck from the word standing before it.

parts.note: OP is the short form of opus, a work — the abbreviation printed before a composer's numbers
the academic is a PROFESSOR, and the O and the F that 'of' names are struck out of it

explanation.surface: An academic writing up the way a tyrant was got rid of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work on academic' reads as one phrase, pressure applied to a scholar, when 'work' is standing alone as OP — the opus number printed on a piece of music.
explanation.definitionFit: An OPPRESSOR is one who holds a people down by force, which is what a tyrant does to those he rules.

clue.text: By way of review, minus changes

indicators.note: A thing that changes does not stay as it was, so the five letters beside it come out in a different order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters

explanation.surface: An accountant summing up now that the deductions have shifted.
explanation.walkthrough: The theme word is doing the hiding: 'minus' looks like an accountant's term in a sentence about figures, and it is five letters waiting to be shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: IN SUM introduces a summing-up — 'in sum, we were wrong' — which is the phrase a reviewer uses to gather everything into one verdict.

clue.text: River trade subtracting tax at the end

indicators.note: Subtracting is taking away, so what it names comes off the word rather than being added to it.
'At the end' says where the doomed letters were sitting: the last three, not the first.

parts.note: trade in the wide sense of commerce and manufacture, the long word to be trimmed
to tax someone is to try them, the way a tiresome child tries your patience

explanation.surface: Riverside commerce with the duty taken off at the end of the year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River trade' reads as one thing, cargo moving on the water, and only 'River' is the definition. The rest turns on tax meaning try — trying behaviour taxes your patience.
explanation.definitionFit: The INDUS is the great river of Pakistan that gave India its name, so 'River' defines it by the class it belongs to.

clue.text: In kinky sex and vice you are audibly digressing

indicators.note: A kink is a twist, and letters described as twisted are letters bent out of the order they arrived in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters; the 'and' only joins them

indicators.note: 'Audibly' asks you to hear the words rather than read them, so what goes in the grid is what they sound like.

parts.note: said aloud, those two words are simply the names of two letters, and the pair joins the shuffle

explanation.surface: Telling somebody that their talk of kinky sex and vice is wandering off the subject.
explanation.walkthrough: U and R come from hearing 'you are' rather than reading it, which is worth keeping: those two letters are otherwise almost impossible to clue.
explanation.definitionFit: EXCURSIVE describes talk that keeps making excursions away from its subject, which is what a digressing speaker does.

clue.text: Mostly rude, mostly unfriendly, totally foolish

indicators.note: 'Mostly' means all but a little, and the little left behind is the final letter of the word it governs.
The second one does the same job on the next word, docking its last letter before the two pieces are laid end to end.

parts.note: rude is IMPOLITE, and most of that is everything but the E
unfriendly is ICY, and most of ICY is its first two letters
surface only, and the setter's joke as well: two mostlys laid end to end come to a totally

explanation.surface: A verdict on somebody who is rude, cold and stupid with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foolish' is doing all the defining on its own, and the word in front of it belongs to the insult in the surface. IMPOLITIC is the political sort of foolish: ill-judged rather than dim.
explanation.definitionFit: IMPOLITIC means ill-judged — the foolishness of a move that will cost you, not stupidity of mind.

clue.text: Parts of speech using negative pieces from Sun

parts.note: the plainest negative in the language, and the one crosswords reach for first

indicators.note: Something in pieces has been broken apart, and the bits never go back in the order they came out.

parts.note: anagram fodder, three letters

explanation.surface: Grammar assembled out of the gloomy fragments printed in a tabloid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Negative pieces' looks like one phrase, dispiriting articles in a newspaper, and it is two separate instructions — while the Sun here is only three letters long.
explanation.definitionFit: NOUNS belong to the set of word classes grammarians call the parts of speech, so the definition names them by their category, in the plural.

clue.text: More or less inaccurate guess upset this team in red

indicators.note: To upset something is to tip it over and spill it, and letters spilled do not land in the order they were stacked.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
red is rouge — the French word, familiar in English as the name of the red make-up

explanation.surface: A wild guess at how badly the team in red were beaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This team in red' looks like a football side you are meant to identify, Liverpool or Arsenal, and nothing needs naming: red is simply rouge.
explanation.definitionFit: A ROUGH ESTIMATE is a figure arrived at approximately, so 'more or less inaccurate' is fair — near enough, and knowingly not exact.

clue.text: Remarks that may require revisions, up or down

definitions.meaning: read it as re-marks: an examiner going through the same pile of papers a second time
a forecast or a valuation revised in either direction

explanation.surface: Comments on a report that might have to be written again.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen you cannot see is the joke: 'Remarks' is re-marks, and marks are assessments, so marking again is doing them again.
explanation.definitionFit: Marks are assessments, so re-marking a script is doing them over; and a figure revised up or down has been judged afresh.

clue.text: Against being briefly affirmative in written opinion

indicators.note: 'In' is the instruction to bury one piece inside another instead of setting it alongside.

parts.note: an op-ed is the newspaper page opposite the editorial, where signed opinion pieces run
affirmative is POSITIVE, and 'briefly' docks it to its first three letters

explanation.surface: Somebody coming out against a cautiously upbeat newspaper column.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Against being briefly affirmative' reads as one continuous grumble about half-hearted praise, and the definition is the first word by itself.
explanation.definitionFit: To be OPPOSED to something is to be against it — the same relation, put as a participle where the clue offers a preposition.

clue.text: Plus ça change with European medicine

indicators.note: 'Change' belongs to the French tag in the surface, and taken as an instruction it says these letters will not stay as they are.

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters; the cedilla is not a letter and drops away
E is the standing abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: The French shrug that the more things change, the more they stay the same.
explanation.walkthrough: Plus ça change is the opening of the French tag about nothing really changing, and the setter has used a quotation as fodder with its own verb as the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A CAPSULE is the small soluble case a dose is packed into, so 'medicine' defines it by what it carries rather than what it is.

clue.text: Shine with half-century in fluctuating game

indicators.note: Something fluctuating will not hold still, and letters that will not hold still do not keep their order.

parts.note: a century is C, a hundred in Roman numerals, and half of it is fifty — L; in cricket a half-century is a batter's fifty runs
anagram fodder, four letters

explanation.surface: A batter's fifty lighting up a match that keeps swinging one way then the other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shine with half-century' reads as one cricketing phrase, a fifty catching the light, and the definition is the first word standing on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A GLEAM is a brief shine of light, and as a verb to gleam is simply to shine.

clue.text: Positive about asset's small excesses

indicators.note: 'About' puts one word round the outside of another, the way arms go about a waist.

parts.note: positive in the sense of certain — 'I'm positive' — gives SURE
an asset is a plus, something on the credit side; the possessive belongs to the surface
S is the standing abbreviation for small, as on a clothing label

explanation.surface: An accountant reporting that a modest asset has left money over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Positive' is the theme word doing double duty: in the surface it sits with the assets, in the wordplay it is nothing but a synonym for sure.
explanation.definitionFit: A SURPLUS is what is left when there is more than was needed, so 'excesses' names the plural of exactly that.

clue.text: Soften line, something that artist can work on

definitions.text: something that artist can work on

parts.note: to ease a rule or a pain is to soften it
L is the standing abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: An instruction to a painter to soften that line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soften line' reads as advice to a painter, which is the misdirection: they are two separate pieces, and the artist belongs only to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An EASEL is the frame a painter stands a canvas on, so it is literally the thing an artist works at.

clue.text: Some overnight for this and others turning up quickly go

indicators.note: In a down entry 'up' points back towards the start, so the letters just named are written in from the bottom.

parts.note: 'and others' after a name in a list is et al, and those four letters are then read the other way
to shift is to move fast — 'shift it!' shouted at somebody dawdling

explanation.surface: Staff who come in overnight for this job and others, then leave in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: Et al is the Latin tag that follows a name in a reference list, standing for 'and others', and here it is four letters to be read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A LATE SHIFT is the working stretch that runs on into the night, so 'Some overnight' picks out the part of the night that gets worked.

clue.text: Setter's beginning — isn't fancy, or as good as Paul (or Brendan)?

indicators.note: 'Beginning' asks for the opening letter alone of the word standing in front of it.

parts.note: the opening letter of the word Setter
ain't is the colloquial form of isn't, and its apostrophe gets no square in the grid
to fancy something is to like it

explanation.surface: One Guardian setter wondering aloud whether he is as virtuous as another.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul and Brendan are both Guardian setters and both saints, which is the joke, and 'fancy' looks like an anagram indicator when it is a straight synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: SAINTLIKE means having the goodness of a saint, and St Paul and St Brendan are named as examples rather than as the quality itself.

clue.text: Adding fix minus bugs

indicators.note: To fix something is to put it right by rearranging its parts, and that is what happens to the nine letters after it.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A software patch that gets rid of the bugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fix minus bugs' reads as a patch with the faults taken out, so 'minus' looks like an instruction to delete something when both words are plain fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: SUBSUMING is taking something in under a wider heading — adding it to a category rather than merely piling it on top.

clue.text: One sequence of notes being performed in which person's unaccompanied

definitions.note: The setter defines by description rather than by synonym: these words are a relative clause naming the state a lone person is in, not a noun you could swap straight into a sentence.

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral
so, la and ti are three consecutive notes of the sol-fa scale, taken in that order
a show being performed is on

explanation.surface: A single passage of music played by somebody with no accompanist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One sequence of notes' reads as a single tune, which is the misdirection: 'One' stands alone, and the notes are sol-fa syllables rather than music.
explanation.definitionFit: ISOLATION is the state of being cut off from other people, which is precisely where a person with nobody alongside them is.

clue.text: Revolutionary device for playing truant out of order — nearly ran

indicators.note: Something out of order is not in the sequence it should be, and that is what becomes of the letters beside it.
'Nearly' means you stop just short, so the last letter of the word it governs never arrives.

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters
a colour that ran BLED, and stopping short of the end leaves three of those letters

explanation.surface: A rebel's gadget for bunking off school, broken and only just going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' wants to be a rebel and is literal instead — a device that revolves — while 'ran' is dye running in the wash, which is bleeding.
explanation.definitionFit: A TURNTABLE is the platter that spins a record, so 'Revolutionary device' describes it by the single thing it does: turn.

clue.text: Go over something obvious left

definitions.meaning: to pass from one side of something to the other
the mark somebody puts on a page in place of a signature — plain to see, and still there on the paper afterwards

explanation.surface: An instruction to check the obvious thing somebody has left behind.
explanation.walkthrough: The theme is what makes the second sense fair: this shape is a plus sign, and two of them are drawn in the black squares of the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: CROSS is the verb for going over something and the noun for the mark left by a person who cannot sign their name — visible at a glance.

clue.text: Indication to remove awful clue, not easy to see

parts.note: the sign written in front of a number to say take it away

indicators.note: Calling the clue awful says its letters are in a state they should not be in, and they get re-laid.

parts.note: anagram fodder, four letters

explanation.surface: An editor demanding that a dreadful, murky clue be cut.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is describing his own trade — an awful clue nobody can see the point of — and the opening three words name the minus sign this puzzle keeps returning to.
explanation.definitionFit: MINUSCULE means very small indeed, and something that small is exactly what is not easy to see.

clue.text: Somewhat unorthodox position of negative pole

indicators.note: 'Somewhat' means to some extent, so what is wanted is part of the word beside it — a run of letters inside, not the whole thing.

parts.note: five letters in a row, starting one letter in and stopping four short of the end

explanation.surface: An unconventional view of where a magnet's minus end sits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unorthodox' looks like an anagram indicator and is the hiding place instead, with the short word in front of it doing all the instructing.
explanation.definitionFit: NORTH is a compass position, and the earth's pole up there attracts a magnet's north end, so it behaves as a south — the negative one.

clue.text: Positive contribution, taken out of context randomly

indicators.note: 'Taken out of' says the letters are lifted straight from what follows rather than built up, so you read across the words for them.

parts.note: five letters in a row, running from the middle of the first word over the gap into the second

explanation.surface: A helpful remark quoted out of context and at random.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Randomly' looks like an anagram indicator and is carrier text holding two of the letters, while 'taken out of context' is the setter describing his own extraction.
explanation.definitionFit: An EXTRA is something added beyond what was owed, a bonus — the plus side of a contribution rather than the part that was due.

clue.text: Calm tips from positive pro

indicators.note: Tips are the two extreme ends of a thing, so the outermost letters of the word are the ones taken.

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word positive
a pro is an expert, and an expert is an ace

explanation.surface: Advice on staying calm handed down by an upbeat professional.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Positive pro' reads as one description of a cheerful expert, and the two words take entirely different treatments: one is trimmed to its ends, the other swapped for a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: PEACE is calm in the sense of quiet and freedom from disturbance — the state itself, not a manner of behaving.

clue.text: Luxurious and hot

parts.note: 'and' and 'plus' do the same job: joining one thing to another
H is the standing abbreviation for hot, the letter on the tap

explanation.surface: A hotel room described as luxurious and warm.
explanation.walkthrough: A three-word clue with no indicator at all is working entirely by substitution, and a whole four-letter chunk coming from 'and' is what makes it hard to see.
explanation.definitionFit: PLUSH means richly comfortable — a plush hotel — from the deep-piled velvet fabric of that name.

clue.text: Final points, one of which is negative in its conclusion

definitions.note: The second definition describes rather than substitutes: it points at the pair of connections on an electrical device, one of them marked with a minus, instead of offering a noun for the answer.
definitions.meaning: the ends of a line, where a railway or a bus route stops

definitions.text: one of which is negative in its conclusion
definitions.meaning: the two connections on a battery, one marked + and one −, and the singular form of the word ends letter for letter in MINUS

explanation.surface: A closing summary whose last item turns out to be a negative one.
explanation.walkthrough: A battery's two ends are its terminals, one of them the minus, and the singular of this word finishes on those very letters — Brendan pointing at his theme inside his own answer.
explanation.definitionFit: TERMINI are end points: of a railway line, or of an electrical device, where the pair are marked positive and negative.

clue.text: Visitor is interrupting perturbed tutor

indicators.note: To interrupt is to break into something already under way, so this piece goes inside the other rather than beside it.
Somebody perturbed has been unsettled, and letters that have been unsettled do not stay in their old order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters
two letters that break into the middle of the shuffled word

explanation.surface: A flustered tutor whose lesson keeps being broken into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' looks like a link word joining a definition to its wordplay, and that is the whole disguise: here it is two letters of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A TOURIST is somebody visiting a place for pleasure, so 'Visitor' is the plain synonym with the holiday sense left implied.

clue.text: Shooting with negative, then positive, results

definitions.text: Shooting with negative, then positive, results

parts.note: the surface hears gunfire, or at best a film crew on location
on film the exposure develops into a negative first, and the print made from that is called a positive — the order the setter is describing

explanation.surface: A shoot that goes badly at first and then comes good.
explanation.walkthrough: Shooting is what a photographer calls it too, and the negative-then-positive sequence is the darkroom's rather than a run of luck.
explanation.definitionFit: Shooting is the photographer's own word for taking pictures, and film yields a negative that is then printed as a positive — the whole clue describes the process.
